claim: Proper chromosome segregation is essential in all living organisms.
source: Proper chromosome segregation is essential in all living organisms.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the importance of chromosome segregation across all domains of life.

claim: Caulobacter crescentus ParB requires cytidine triphosphate to escape the nucleation site parS and spread by sliding to the neighboring DNA.
source: Previously, we showed that Caulobacter crescentus ParB requires cytidine triphosphate to escape the nucleation site parS and spread by sliding to the neighboring DNA (Jalal et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim references a previous study by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Co-crystal structures of a C-terminal domain truncated C. crescentus ParB with parS and with a CTP analog were solved.
source: Here, we provide the structural basis for this transition from nucleation to spreading by solving co-crystal structures of a C-terminal domain truncated C. crescentus ParB with parS and with a CTP analog.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the crystallographic structures.

claim: Nucleating ParB is an open clamp, in which parS is captured at the DNA-binding domain (the DNA-gate).
source: Nucleating ParB is an open clamp, in which parS is captured at the DNA-binding domain (the DNA-gate).
evidence: This claim is based on structural data from the ParB-parS co-crystal structure presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upon binding CTP, the N-terminal domain (NTD) self-dimerizes to close the NTD-gate of the clamp.
source: Upon binding CTP, the N-terminal domain (NTD) self-dimerizes to close the NTD-gate of the clamp.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the ParB-CTPγS co-crystal structure.

claim: The DNA-gate closes upon CTP binding, thus driving parS into a compartment between the DNA-gate and the C-terminal domain.
source: The DNA-gate also closes, thus driving parS into a compartment between the DNA-gate and the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparisons and crosslinking experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: CTP hydrolysis and/or the release of hydrolytic products are likely associated with reopening of the gates to release DNA and recycle ParB.
source: CTP hydrolysis and/or the release of hydrolytic products are likely associated with reopening of the gates to release DNA and recycle ParB.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the characterization of the E102A mutant and other experimental observations.

claim: ParB nucleates on parS before spreading to adjacent non-specific DNA to form a higher-order nucleoprotein complex.
source: ParB, a CTPase and DNA-binding protein, nucleates on parS before spreading to adjacent non-specific DNA to form a higher-order nucleoprotein complex (Breier and Grossman, 2007; Broedersz et al., 2014; Graham et al., 2014; Jalal and Le, 2020a; Murray et al., 2006; Rodionov et al., 1999; Sanchez et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The ParB-DNA nucleoprotein complex stimulates the ATPase activity of ParA, driving the movement of the parS locus to the opposite pole of the cell.
source: The ParB-DNA nucleoprotein complex stimulates the ATPase activity of ParA, driving the movement of the parS locus (and subsequently, the whole chromosome) to the opposite pole of the cell (Hwang et al., 2013; Leonard et al., 2005; Lim et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2021; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014; Vecchiarelli et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: ParB spreads by sliding along the DNA in a manner that depends on the binding of cytidine triphosphate (CTP).
source: ParB spreads by sliding along the DNA, in a manner that depends on the binding of a co-factor, cytidine triphosphate (CTP) (Balaguer F de et al., 2021; Jalal et al., 2020c; Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: A co-crystal structure of a C-terminal domain truncated Bacillus subtilis ParB together with CDP showed the nucleotide to be sandwiched between adjacent subunits, thus promoting their dimerization.
source: A co-crystal structure of a C-terminal domain truncated Bacillus subtilis ParB (ParB∆CTD) together with CDP showed the nucleotide to be sandwiched between adjacent subunits, thus promoting their dimerization (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: A similar arrangement was seen in the co-crystal structure of an N-terminal domain (NTD) truncated version of the Myxococcus xanthus ParB homolog, PadC, bound to CTP.
source: A similar arrangement was seen in the co-crystal structure of an N-terminal domain (NTD) truncated version of the Myxococcus xanthus ParB homolog, PadC, bound to CTP (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Self-dimerization at the NTD of B. subtilis ParB creates a clamp-like molecule that enables DNA entrapment.
source: Self-dimerization at the NTD of B. subtilis ParB creates a clamp-like molecule that enables DNA entrapment (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: CTP facilitates the dissociation of ParB from parS, thereby switching ParB from a nucleating mode to a sliding mode.
source: Biochemical studies with M. xanthus and C. crescentus ParBs showed that CTP facilitates the dissociation of ParB from parS, thereby switching ParB from a nucleating mode to a sliding mode (Jalal et al., 2020c; Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: ParB can hydrolyze CTP to CDP and inorganic phosphate.
source: ParB can hydrolyze CTP to CDP and inorganic phosphate (Jalal et al., 2020c; Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019);
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: CTP hydrolysis is not required for spreading since ParB in complex with a non-hydrolyzable CTP analog (CTPɣS) can still self-load and slide on DNA.
source: however, hydrolysis is not required for spreading since ParB in complex with a non-hydrolyzable CTP analog (CTPɣS) can still self-load and slide on DNA (Jalal et al., 2020c; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: M. xanthus PadC does not possess noticeable CTPase activity.
source: Furthermore, M. xanthus PadC does not possess noticeable CTPase activity (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The role of CTP hydrolysis in bacterial chromosome segregation is not yet clear.
source: As such, the role of CTP hydrolysis in bacterial chromosome segregation is not yet clear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the ParB∆CTD-parS co-crystal contains four copies of ParB∆CTD and two copies of the parS DNA.
source: The asymmetric unit contains four copies of ParB∆CTD and two copies of the parS DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and referenced figures.

claim: Each ParB∆CTD subunit consists of an NTD (helices α1–α4 and sheets β1–β4) and a DBD (helices α5–α10).
source: Each ParB∆CTD subunit consists of an NTD (helices α1–α4 and sheets β1–β4) and a DBD (helices α5–α10) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the co-crystal structure.

claim: Each ParB∆CTD binds to a half parS site, but there is no protein-protein contact between the two adjacent subunits.
source: Each ParB∆CTD binds to a half parS site, but there is no protein-protein contact between the two adjacent subunits (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the co-crystal structure.

claim: The NTDs of ParB from C. crescentus and H. pylori can adopt multiple alternative orientations.
source: Furthermore, by superimposing the C. crescentus ParB∆CTD-parS structure onto that of Helicobacter pylori (Chen et al., 2015), we observed that the NTDs of ParB from both species can adopt multiple alternative orientations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ability of the NTD to adopt multiple open conformations is likely a general feature of nucleating ParB.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the ability of the NTD to adopt multiple open conformations is likely a general feature of nucleating ParB.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparisons across different species.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the ParB∆CTD-CTPɣS co-crystal contains two copies of ParB∆CTD, each with a CTPɣS molecule and a coordinated Mg2+ ion bound at the NTD.
source: The asymmetric unit contains two copies of ParB∆CTD, each with a CTPɣS molecule and a coordinated Mg2+ ion bound at the NTD (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and referenced figures.

claim: Nucleotide-bound NTDs from opposite subunits self-dimerize, thus adopting a closed conformation.
source: In contrast to the open conformation of the ParB∆CTD-parS structure, nucleotide-bound NTDs from opposite subunits self-dimerize (with an interface area of 2111 Å2, as determined by PISA; Krissinel, 2015), thus adopting a closed conformation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the co-crystal structure.

claim: Multiple CTPɣS-contacting residues also directly contribute to the NTD self-dimerization interface.
source: Multiple CTPɣS-contacting residues also directly contribute to the NTD self-dimerization interface (summarized in Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating a coupling between nucleotide binding and self-dimerization.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The closed conformation at the NTD is structurally conserved in nucleotide-bound ParB/ParB-like proteins.
source: Furthermore, the C. crescentus ParB∆CTD-CTPɣS structure is similar to that of the CDP-bound B. subtilis ParB∆CTD (RMSD = 1.48 Å) and the CTP-bound M. xanthus PadC∆NTD (RMSD = 2.23 Å) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), suggesting that the closed conformation at the NTD is structurally conserved in nucleotide-bound ParB/ParB-like proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparisons across different species.

claim: Ten amino acids form hydrogen-bonding contacts with three phosphate groups of CTPɣS, either directly or via the coordinated Mg2+ ion.
source: Ten amino acids form hydrogen-bonding contacts with three phosphate groups of CTPɣS, either directly or via the coordinated Mg2+ ion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the co-crystal structure.

claim: Four amino acids at helix α1 and the α1–β2 intervening loop provide hydrogen-bonding interactions to the cytosine ring.
source: Four amino acids at helix α1 and the α1–β2 intervening loop provide hydrogen-bonding interactions to the cytosine ring, hence are termed the C-motif (C for cytosine motif, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the co-crystal structure.

claim: Six additional residues contact the ribose moiety and/or the pyrimidine moiety via hydrophobic interactions.
source: Lastly, six additional residues contact the ribose moiety and/or the pyrimidine moiety via hydrophobic interactions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the co-crystal structure.

claim: The C-motif forms a snug fit to the pyrimidine moiety, thus is incompatible with larger purine moieties such as those from ATP or GTP.
source: The C-motif forms a snug fit to the pyrimidine moiety, thus is incompatible with larger purine moieties such as those from ATP or GTP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing the specificity of the binding pocket.

claim: Hydrogen-bonding contacts from the G79 main chain and the S74 side chain to the amino group at position 4 of the cytosine moiety further distinguish CTP from UTP.
source: Hydrogen-bonding contacts from the G79 main chain and the S74 side chain to the amino group at position 4 of the cytosine moiety further distinguish CTP from UTP (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the co-crystal structure.

claim: The structural data are consistent with the known specificity of C. crescentus ParB for CTP.
source: Taken all together, our structural data are consistent with the known specificity of C. crescentus ParB for CTP (Jalal et al., 2020c).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and a citation to published research.

claim: In the nucleating state, helices α3 and α4 from each subunit bundle together (32° angle between α3 and α4).
source: In the nucleating state, as represented by the ParB∆CTD-parS structure, helices α3 and α4 from each subunit bundle together (32o angle between α3 and α4, Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the co-crystal structure.

claim: In the spreading state, α3 swings outwards by 101° to pack itself with α4′ from the opposing subunit.
source: However, in the spreading state, as represented by the ParB∆CTD-CTPɣS structure, α3 swings outwards by 101o to pack itself with α4′ from the opposing subunit (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the co-crystal structure.

claim: Nucleotide binding most likely facilitates the 'swinging-out' conformation since both α3 and the α3–α4 loop make numerous contacts with the bound CTPɣS and the coordinated Mg2+ ion.
source: Nucleotide binding most likely facilitates this 'swinging-out' conformation since both α3 and the α3–α4 loop, that is, P-motif 3 make numerous contacts with the bound CTPɣS and the coordinated Mg2+ ion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data showing the interactions between the protein and nucleotide.

claim: Residues 44–121 at the NTD rotate wholesale by 94° to dimerize with their counterpart from the opposing subunit.
source: Indeed, residues 44–121 at the NTD rotate wholesale by 94o to dimerize with their counterpart from the opposing subunit (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparisons between the two states.

claim: Residues 161–221 at the DBD rotate upward by 26° in a near rigid-body movement.
source: Also, residues 161–221 at the DBD rotate upward by 26o in a near rigid-body movement (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparisons between the two states.

claim: The opposite DBDs are closer together in the spreading state (inter-domain distance = ~ 27 Å) than in the nucleating state (inter-domain distance = ~ 36 Å).
source: As a result, the opposite DBDs are closer together in the spreading state (inter-domain distance = ~ 27 Å) than in the nucleating state (inter-domain distance = ~ 36 Å) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural measurements from the co-crystal structures.

claim: The DBDs in the spreading state clash severely with DNA, hence are no longer compatible with parS DNA binding.
source: By overlaying the CTPɣS-bound structure onto the parS DNA complex, it is clear that the DBDs in the spreading state clash severely with DNA, hence are no longer compatible with parS DNA binding (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural superposition analysis.

claim: The structural data are consistent with the previous finding that CTP decreases C. crescentus ParB nucleation on parS or liberates pre-bound ParB from parS site.
source: Our structural data are therefore consistent with the previous finding that CTP decreases C. crescentus ParB nucleation on parS or liberates pre-bound ParB from parS site (Jalal et al., 2020c).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and a citation to published research.

claim: CTP binding stabilizes a conformation that is incompatible with DNA-binding and this change might facilitate ParB escape from the high-affinity nucleation parS site.
source: Overall, we suggest that CTP binding stabilizes a conformation that is incompatible with DNA-binding and that this change might facilitate ParB escape from the high-affinity nucleation parS site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and biochemical observations.

claim: The crosslinking of both ParB (Q35C) and ParB (L224C) was enhanced ~2.5–3-fold in the presence of parS DNA and CTP.
source: We observed that the crosslinking of both ParB (Q35C) and ParB (L224C) was enhanced ~2.5–3-fold in the presence of parS DNA and CTP (Figure 5B), consistent with CTP favoring a conformation when the NTD and the DBD are close together.
evidence: This claim is supported by crosslinking experimental data.

claim: ParB (I304C) crosslinked independently of CTP or parS, supporting the known role of the CTD as a primary dimerization domain.
source: In contrast, ParB (I304C) crosslinked independently of CTP or parS (Figure 5B), supporting the known role of the CTD as a primary dimerization domain (Figge et al., 2003; Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by crosslinking experimental data and citations to published research.

claim: C. crescentus ParB dimer functions as a molecular clamp that entraps parS-containing DNA within a DBD-CTD compartment upon CTP binding.
source: Taken together, we suggest that C. crescentus ParB dimer functions as a molecular clamp that entraps parS-containing DNA within a DBD-CTD compartment upon CTP binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by double crosslinking experiments and structural data.

claim: A premature and irreversible closing of ParB clamps prevented nucleation at parS and DNA entrapment.
source: This is also consistent with experiments that showed a premature and irreversible closing of ParB clamps, achieved either by an extended preincubation with CTPɣS (Jalal et al., 2020c and Figure 5—figure supplement 4B) or by pre-crosslinking a closed clamp form of ParB (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C), prevented nucleation at parS and DNA entrapment.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: ParB (E102A) is a clamp-locked mutant that is defective in CTP hydrolysis but otherwise competent in NTD self-dimerization.
source: We postulated that creation of a ParB variant defective in CTP hydrolysis but otherwise competent in NTD self-dimerization would enable us to investigate the possible role of CTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by alanine scanning mutagenesis and subsequent biochemical characterization.

claim: ParB (E102A) binds CTP with similar affinity to wild-type ParB.
source: Figure 6A
evidence: The membrane-spotting assay in Figure 6A shows that ParB (E102A) binds CTP, indicating it retains CTP binding ability.

claim: ParB (E102A) is defective in CTP hydrolysis.
source: Figure 6B
evidence: The inorganic phosphate release assay in Figure 6B shows that ParB (E102A) has minimal CTPase activity compared to wild-type.

claim: ParB (E102A) is competent in NTD self-dimerization.
source: Figure 6C
evidence: The crosslinking assay in Figure 6C shows that ParB (E102A) can undergo NTD self-dimerization in the presence of CTP.

claim: Entrapped ParB (E102A) did not noticeably dissociate from a closed DNA substrate when the probe was returned to a buffer-only solution.
source: Upon a closer inspection of the BLI sensorgrams (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and Figure 7), we noted that the entrapped ParB (E102A) did not noticeably dissociate from a closed DNA substrate when the probe was returned to a buffer-only solution (dissociation phase, koff = 8.0 × 10–4 ± 1.9 × 10–4 s–1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: Entrapped ParB (WT) dissociated approximately 15-fold faster into buffer than ParB (E102A).
source: By contrast, entrapped ParB (WT) dissociated approximately 15-fold faster into buffer (koff = 1.2 × 10–2 ± 3.7 × 10–4 s–1).
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: DNA entrapment by ParB (E102A) is more tolerant to high-salt solution (up to 1 M NaCl) than ParB (WT).
source: Further experiments showed that DNA entrapment by ParB (E102A), unlike ParB (WT), is more tolerant to high-salt solution (up to 1 M NaCl, Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: ParB (E102A)-CTP could not accumulate on a BamHI-restricted open DNA substrate.
source: Nevertheless, ParB (E102A)-CTP could not accumulate on a BamHI-restricted open DNA substrate (Figure 7B,C; Jalal et al., 2020c), suggesting that ParB (E102A)-CTP, similar to ParB (WT), also form a closed clamp that runs off an open DNA end.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: parS DNA and CTP induced a stably closed clamp conformation of ParB (E102A) in vitro.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that parS DNA and CTP induced a stably closed clamp conformation of ParB (E102A) in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BLI and crosslinking experimental data.

claim: The ChIP-seq profile of FLAG-ParB (WT) showed an ~10 kb region of enrichment above background with clearly defined peaks that correspond to the positions of parS sites.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Tran et al., 2018), the ChIP-seq profile of FLAG-ParB (WT) showed an ~10 kb region of enrichment above background with clearly defined peaks that correspond to the positions of parS sites (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq experimental data and a citation to published research.

claim: The ChIP-seq profile of FLAG-ParB (E102A) is significantly reduced in height but has an extra peak over the parB coding sequence.
source: By contrast, the ChIP-seq profile of FLAG-ParB (E102A) is significantly reduced in height but has an extra peak over the parB coding sequence (Figure 8A, asterisk).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq experimental data.

claim: The instability of FLAG-ParB (E102A) in its native C. crescentus host might explain the overall lower height of its ChIP-seq profile.
source: The instability of FLAG-ParB (E102A) in its native C. crescentus host, and hence the reduced protein level (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), might explain the overall lower height of its ChIP-seq profile (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunoblot and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Expressing ParB (E102A) could not rescue cells with depleted ParB (WT).
source: We also noted that expressing ParB (E102A) could not rescue cells with depleted ParB (WT) (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell viability experimental data.

claim: CFP-ParB (WT) in an E. coli host spreads asymmetrically ~5 kb around parS sites.
source: We observed by ChIP-seq that CFP-ParB (WT) in an E. coli host spreads asymmetrically ~5 kb around parS sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq experimental data in E. coli.

claim: The shape of the ParB (E102A) distribution was clearly different from that of ParB (WT); the profile was further expanded to both neighboring sides of parS (covering in total ~26 kb) at the expense of the enrichment at parS itself.
source: By contrast, the shape of the ParB (E102A) distribution was clearly different from that of ParB (WT); the profile was further expanded to both neighboring sides of parS (covering in total ~26 kb) at the expense of the enrichment at parS itself (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq experimental data in E. coli.

claim: The more excessive spreading of ParB (E102A) might suggest that this variant, in the absence of CTP hydrolysis, persisted and perhaps slid further away from the loading site parS in E. coli.
source: The more excessive spreading of ParB (E102A) might suggest that this variant, in the absence of CTP hydrolysis, persisted and perhaps slid further away from the loading site parS in E. coli.
evidence: This is speculation based on the ChIP-seq data.

claim: The reduced enrichment of ParB (E102A) at parS itself might be due to reduced cytoplasmic ParB (E102A) available to re-nucleate at parS and/or due to stably entrapped ParB (E102A) sterically hindering further nucleation events.
source: The reduced enrichment of ParB (E102A) at parS itself (Figure 8B) might be due to reduced cytoplasmic ParB (E102A) available to re-nucleate at parS and/or due to stably entrapped ParB (E102A) sterically hindering further nucleation events.
evidence: This is speculation based on the ChIP-seq data.

claim: The ChIP-seq profile of CFP-ParB (E102A) in E. coli is highly asymmetrical, with more enrichment in the 2905–2911 kb region than the 2885–2899 kb region.
source: We also noted that the ChIP-seq profile of CFP-ParB (E102A) in E. coli is highly asymmetrical, with more enrichment in the 2905–2911 kb region than the 2885–2899 kb region (shaded areas, Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq experimental data in E. coli.

claim: The asymmetrical spreading is possibly due to an impediment in one direction by roadblocks such as RNA polymerases or DNA-bound proteins.
source: The asymmetrical spreading is possibly due to an impediment in one direction by roadblocks such as RNA polymerases or DNA-bound proteins, which have been shown previously to be able to interfere with ParB spreading (Balaguer F de et al., 2021; Breier and Grossman, 2007; Jalal et al., 2020c; Murray et al., 2006; Rodionov et al., 1999; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation based on the ChIP-seq data and citations to published research.

claim: CFP-ParB (E102A) foci have higher fluorescence intensity than CFP-ParB (WT) foci inside E. coli cells.
source: Lastly, we quantified the fluorescence intensity of CFP-ParB (WT/E102A) foci inside cells and found a higher CFP signal for CFP-ParB (E102A) when compared with CFP-ParB (WT) (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy experimental data.

claim: The higher intensity of the localizations could be due to more DNA-bound ParB (E102A) molecules surrounding the parS locus.
source: The higher intensity of the localizations could be due to more DNA-bound ParB (E102A) molecules surrounding the parS locus, which is consistent with the ChIP-seq observation showing CFP-ParB (E102A) occupying a more extended genomic area in E. coli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence microscopy and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The 'clamp-locked' phenotype of ParB (E102A) implies a possible role of CTP hydrolysis and/or the release of hydrolytic products in reopening wild-type ParB clamp to release DNA and to recycle ParB.
source: Altogether, at least in the heterologous E. coli host, the 'clamp-locked' phenotype of ParB (E102A) implies a possible role of CTP hydrolysis and/or the release of hydrolytic products in reopening wild-type ParB clamp to release DNA and to recycle ParB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characterization of ParB (E102A) in E. coli.

claim: Nucleating ParB is an open clamp in which parS DNA is held tightly (nM affinity) at the DBD.
source: Nucleating ParB is an open clamp in which parS DNA is held tightly (nM affinity) at the DBD (Tran et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and a citation to published research.

claim: The NTDs of nucleating ParB can adopt multiple alternative conformations, and crucially there is no contact between opposing NTDs.
source: The NTDs of nucleating ParB can adopt multiple alternative conformations, and crucially there is no contact between opposing NTDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: In the sliding state, CTP promotes the self-dimerization of the NTDs, thus closing the NTD-gate.
source: In the sliding state, CTP promotes the self-dimerization of the NTDs, thus closing the NTD-gate (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: Opposing DBDs also move approximately 10 Å closer together, bringing about a conformation that is DNA incompatible.
source: Opposing DBDs also move approximately 10 Å closer together, bringing about a conformation that is DNA incompatible.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The DNA-gate closure explains how CTP binding might switch ParB from a nucleating to a sliding state.
source: Overall, the DNA-gate closure explains how CTP binding might switch ParB from a nucleating to a sliding state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The closure of the two gates drives parS DNA into a compartment in between the DBD and the CTD.
source: Our data suggest that the closure of the two gates drives parS DNA into a compartment in between the DBD and the CTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and crosslinking experiments.

claim: The linker that connects the DBD and the CTD together is invariably ~20 amino acid in length and positively charged lysines are over-represented.
source: The linker that connects the DBD and the CTD together is not conserved in amino acid sequence among chromosomal ParB orthologs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2); however, we noted that the linker is invariably ~20 amino acid in length and positively charged lysines are over-represented (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: parS DNA promotes the CTP-dependent NTD-gate closure.
source: In this study, we showed that parS DNA promotes the CTP-dependent NTD-gate closure (Figure 5B), thus is likely a built-in mechanism to ensure gate closure results in a productive DNA entrapment.
evidence: This claim is supported by crosslinking experimental data.

claim: CTP functions as a molecular latch that stabilizes the closure of the NTD-gate of ParB.
source: CTP functions as a molecular latch that stabilizes the closure of the NTD-gate of ParB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: CTP hydrolysis might contribute to reopening the closed NTD-gate.
source: Here, we provide evidence that CTP hydrolysis might contribute to reopening the closed NTD-gate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characterization of the E102A mutant.

claim: Both CTP hydrolysis and the subsequent release of hydrolytic products are necessary to reopen the gates.
source: A previous structure of a B. subtilis ParB∆CTD-CDP complex also has its NTD-gate closed (CTP was hydrolyzed to CDP during the crystallization) (Soh et al., 2019), hence it is likely that both CTP hydrolysis and the subsequent release of hydrolytic products are necessary to reopen the gates.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural data and a citation to published research.

claim: ParB has a weak to negligible affinity for CDP.
source: However, ParB has a weak to negligible affinity for CDP, hence the CDP-bound ParB species might be short-lived in solution and might not play a significant biological role.
evidence: This is an inference based on biochemical properties.

claim: Once the clamp is reopened, entrapped DNA might escape via the same route that it first enters.
source: Once the clamp is reopened, entrapped DNA might escape via the same route that it first enters.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural model.

claim: The CTDs of ParB are stably dimerized independently of parS and CTP.
source: However, the CTDs of ParB are stably dimerized independently of parS and CTP (Figure 5B), hence we speculate that the CTD of ParB is likely to be impassable to the entrapped DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by crosslinking experimental data.

claim: A recycling mechanism might provide a biological advantage since a ParB clamp once closed could otherwise become stably trapped on DNA and thus eventually diffuse too far from the parS locus.
source: Such a recycling mechanism might provide a biological advantage since a ParB clamp once closed could otherwise become stably trapped on DNA and thus eventually diffuse too far from the parS locus, as evidenced by the ChIP-seq profile of the E102A variant (expressed in E. coli) that is defective in CTP hydrolysis (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is speculation based on the ChIP-seq data of the E102A mutant.

claim: Q58 (P-motif 1) and E102 (P-motif 2) might be involved in the catalytic mechanism of C. crescentus ParB.
source: Nevertheless, based on our alanine scanning experiment (Figure 8), we speculate that Q58 (P-motif 1) and E102 (P-motif 2) might be involved in the catalytic mechanism of C. crescentus ParB.
evidence: This is speculation based on the alanine scanning mutagenesis data.

claim: An equivalent Q37 in B. subtilis ParB does not contact the hydrolytic product CDP.
source: Supporting this view, we noted that an equivalent Q37 in B. subtilis ParB does not contact the hydrolytic product CDP, and this residue is not conserved in the catalytic-dead M. xanthus PadC (F308, which does not contact CTP, occupies this position in PadC instead) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparisons.

claim: E102 is not conserved in M. xanthus PadC (F348 occupies this equivalent position).
source: E102 is also not conserved in M. xanthus PadC (F348 occupies this equivalent position) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparisons.

claim: An F-plasmid ParB was shown to form biomolecular condensates in vivo that might bridge distal ParBF dimers together.
source: Recently, an F-plasmid ParB was shown to form biomolecular condensates in vivo that might bridge distal ParBF dimers together (Guilhas et al., 2020; Walter et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Two protomers of a single ParBF dimer interact with a ParAF dimer in the absence of CTP.
source: Recent in vitro work with ParABF showed that two protomers of a single ParBF dimer interact with a ParAF dimer in the absence of CTP (Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Two ParBF protomers from two distinct dimers interact with a ParAF dimer in the presence of CTP and parS.
source: However, two ParBF protomers from two distinct dimers interact with a ParAF dimer in the presence of CTP and parS (Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Diffraction data for the ParB∆CTD-parS co-crystal were collected to 2.9 Å resolution.
source: Diffraction data for the ParB∆CTD-parS co-crystal were collected to 2.9 Å resolution, and the structure was solved by molecular replacement (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: A 2.7 Å resolution structure of C. crescentus ParB∆CTD in complex with CTPɣS was solved.
source: Next, to gain insight into the spreading state of ParB, we solved a 2.7 Å resolution structure of C. crescentus ParB∆CTD in complex with CTPɣS (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The ParB∆CTD-parS complex crystallized in space group P21 with cell parameters of a = 54.3, b = 172.9, c = 72.9 Å, and β = 90.5°.
source: The ParB∆CTD-parS complex crystallized in space group P21 with cell parameters of a = 54.3, b = 172.9, c = 72.9 Å, and β = 90.5° (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The ParB∆CTD-CTPɣS complex crystallized in space group P21 with cell parameters of a = 69.5, b = 56.1, c = 71.4 Å, and β = 98.4°.
source: The ParB∆CTD-CTPɣS complex crystallized in space group P21 with cell parameters of a = 69.5, b = 56.1, c = 71.4 Å, and β = 98.4° (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data.
